chapter.title: Wood and articles of wood; wood charcoal

page.h1: HTS Chapter 44: Wood and articles of wood; wood charcoal — U.S. Exports & Foreign Tariffs

seo.title: U.S. Lumber, Log & Wood Pellet Exports: Top Buyers and Tariffs
seo.shortDescription: The U.S. exported $8.79B of wood in 2025: $1.93B of wood pellets, $2.53B of lumber, $1.42B of logs. Who buys it (Canada, UK, China) and what each charges.

intro:
The U.S. exported **$8.79 billion** of wood and wood products (HTS Chapter 44) in 2025, down **8.1%** from 2024. Three products carry most of it: sawn **lumber** (heading 4407, **$2.53 billion**, led by oak at $873 million and pine at $605 million), **wood pellets** (4401.31, **$1.93 billion**, the largest single line) and **logs** ($1.42 billion). Canada is the largest buyer (**23%**), then the United Kingdom (**19%**, almost all wood pellets), Mexico, China, Viet Nam and Japan.

Most buyers charge little or nothing: logs and lumber enter the EU, the UK, Viet Nam and Japan duty-free (Japan charges 4.8% on S-P-F and pine lumber), the UK and EU take pellets free, and Mexico and Canada take qualifying U.S. wood free under USMCA. The exceptions are **Canada**, which since September 8, 2026 charges U.S. softwood lumber **25%** and plywood and charcoal **50%**, and **China**, which adds **10%** to every U.S. good and suspended U.S. log imports from March 4 to November 10, 2025; U.S. wood sales to China halved to **$806 million** in 2025 while Viet Nam’s doubled. For logs and lumber, what usually decides access is the buyer’s plant-health rules (the USDA phytosanitary certificate, fumigation of logs), and for the EU from December 30, 2026 its deforestation rules.

keyTakeaways: Pellets, lumber and logs are about two-thirds of U.S. Chapter 44 exports. The UK alone bought $1.45 billion of fuel wood and pellets (heading 4401) in 2025, almost all pellets.

Canada is the only buyer that targets U.S. wood: since September 8, 2026 its surtax charges 25% on softwood lumber (4407.11–4407.19) and 50% on plywood, LVL and charcoal, with no CUSMA exemption. Hardwood lumber, logs, pellets and joinery still enter free.

China reopened to U.S. logs on November 10, 2025 and its purchases are recovering (up 25% in January–August 2026), but it still adds 10% to all U.S. goods, and two dates could raise that: December 31, 2026 (tariff exclusions end) and January 10, 2027 (24-point suspension ends).

The EU dropped its duties on all U.S. Chapter 44 goods to 0% from July 1, 2026, which mostly helps panels and plywood (normally 7%); for U.S. pellets and lumber the date that matters is December 30, 2026, when the EU Deforestation Regulation starts to apply.
